target.title: Denoising Convolutional Autoencoder Based B-Mode Ultrasound Tongue Image Feature Extraction

read.pdf: Visually read Figs. 1–3 and Tables 1–2 (PDF pp. 2–4); Fig. 3 shows DCT, AE, and CAE reconstructions.

entries.text: The feature-extraction autoencoders are unsupervised reconstruction models; the paper describes targets as equal to their inputs, with noisy inputs for denoising variants.
entries.condition: Training target/input relationship; DAE/DCAE receive corrupted inputs.

entries.text: The challenge data are mid-sagittal tongue ultrasound at 60 fps, acquired with a stabilizing light helmet and a 4–8 MHz, 128-element microconvex probe beneath the chin.
entries.condition: 2010 Silent Speech Challenge acquisition; mid-sagittal UTI.

entries.text: Raw frames are 320×240 pixels; selected ROIs are bicubically resized to 50×60 before feature extraction.
entries.condition: Preprocessing for feature-extraction experiments; ROI selection procedure is not described.

entries.text: For reconstruction, the authors report 50,000 training and 30,000 test images randomly selected from the Silent Speech Challenge dataset.
entries.condition: Reconstruction evaluation; selection is reported at image level, with no speaker/session partition details.
entries.quote:
We employ 50,000 training images and 30,000
images for test, all of which were randomly selected from the
Silent Speech Challenge dataset.

entries.text: The cited deep-AE benchmark architecture has 3 encoding and 3 decoding layers, with 1000, 500, and 250 hidden units.
entries.condition: Deep-AE benchmark architecture attributed to reference [1].

entries.text: CAE/DCAE use 3 convolutional and 3 max-pooling encoder layers; convolution kernels are 8×8 (32 filters), 6×6 (16 filters), and 4×4 (2 filters).
entries.condition: CAE and DCAE encoder architecture; pooling sizes vary with encoder feature dimension.
entries.quote:
in which the size of ﬁrst convolutional layer is 8 × 8 with 32
ﬁlters

entries.text: DAE/DCAE training adds randomly generated speckle noise and uses Adam at learning rate 0.001 for a fixed 200 epochs.
entries.condition: Paper does not report seeds, batch size, or the exact noise-generation distribution/parameters.

entries.text: The compared encoder sizes include 1×(5,6)=30, 2×(5,6)=60, and for some models 1×(10,6)=60 or 1×(30,1)=30 / 1×(60,1)=60.
entries.condition: Feature length is channels multiplied by map height and width; model-specific sizes appear in Table 1.

entries.text: Recognition uses a DNN-HMM recognizer on concatenated tongue and lip features of total dimension K=60 or 30; the paper inconsistently calls it DMM-HMM once.
entries.condition: Features are extracted by DCT, Deep AE, Denoising AE, CAE, or DCAE; Kaldi implementation. The DNN-HMM/DMM-HMM wording differs within Sec. 3.3.

entries.text: A Wall Street Journal language model is used in the recognition system.
entries.condition: No LM training data version or decoding weights are specified.

entries.text: The paper reports prior work finding AE features comparable to DCT features, with similar recognition performance using fewer feature vectors.
entries.condition: Prior multimodal silent-speech recognition study, cited as [1]; not a result of this paper.

entries.text: The paper states that low-frequency DCT components had outperformed EigenTongue features in previous work.
entries.condition: Background claim attributed to reference [11].

entries.text: The authors argue that convolutional autoencoders may handle noisy, shifted, and corrupted images better than classic deep autoencoders and may remove ultrasound speckle noise.
entries.condition: Rationale/expected behavior; general shift and corruption robustness are not separately quantified in the reported experiments.

entries.text: The authors claim novelty: to their knowledge this is the first use of denoising CAE for feature extraction in ultrasound tongue images.
entries.condition: Novelty claim is not supported by a systematic literature-search method in the paper.
entries.quote:
We be-
lieve this is the ﬁrst attempt to use denoising CAE for fea-
ture extraction in the ultrasound tongue image.

entries.text: The authors say DCAE outperforms the compared feature extractors on reconstruction and the 2010 Silent Speech Interface Challenge.
entries.condition: Their reported evidence is reconstruction MSE/CW-SSIM and Silent Speech Challenge WER; see Tables 1–2.

entries.text: The authors report that CAE and DCAE outperform deep AE on reconstruction by MSE and CW-SSIM, and DCAE performs better than CAE in the same task.
entries.condition: Reconstruction comparison on the reported image test set; numerical results are in Table 1.

entries.text: The authors state that Denoising AE reconstructs better than deep AE, DCT is similar to deep AE at length 30, and error generally falls with longer features except for DCT.
entries.condition: Authors' interpretation of Table 1; not a statistical-significance analysis.
entries.quote:
With the increase
of the feature length, the reconstruction error can be reduced,
except with DCT.

entries.text: The authors report the lowest WER with DCAE and infer that CAEs encode more speech-related information than AEs.
entries.condition: WER comparison on the 2010 Silent Speech Challenge using the stated DNN-HMM and WSJ LM setup.

entries.text: The authors claim convolutional layers should improve robustness to head-motion distortion, differences between imaging systems, and inherent speckle noise; they also claim better spatial preservation and fewer failures across instruments.
entries.condition: Conclusion assertions; dedicated head-motion, instrument-transfer, or robustness subgroup tests are not reported.

entries.text: Ultrasound does not record vocal-source or lip movements; the authors note that lip video can be added to an ultrasound SSI.
entries.condition: Sensing limitation of ultrasound-only capture.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge ultrasound images are high-dimensional and sparse, have low signal-to-noise ratio and speckle contamination, and may be distorted by head movement.
entries.condition: Limitations motivating invariant feature extraction; not all are experimentally isolated here.

entries.text: The authors say sequence autoencoders and alternative dynamic-process models such as recurrent neural networks remain underway.
entries.condition: Current work evaluates frame-level features and does not report these sequence/dynamic models.

entries.text: The measured output is word recognition scored by WER; the paper does not evaluate speech synthesis or reconstructed-speech quality.
entries.condition: 2010 Silent Speech Challenge recognition evaluation; the reported metric is WER.

entries.text: No deployment evaluation, runtime/latency, resource use, usability test, or clinical linguist assessment is reported; clinical usefulness is motivational only.
entries.condition: System use outside the offline benchmark experiments.

entries.text: The abstract compares DCAE's 6.17% WER with a cited state-of-the-art DCT value of 6.45%; Table 2 identifies the latter as the 30-dimensional DCT result.
entries.condition: Prior SOTA comparator attributed to DCT; Table 2 associates 6.45 with feature length 30, whereas DCAE's 6.17 is at length 60, so the abstract comparison is not dimension matched.
entries.quote:
state-of-the-art value of 6.45% using Discrete cosine trans-
form as the feature extractor.

questions.q: Does the reported WER establish a dimension-matched improvement over the cited state of the art?
questions.answer: DCAE has the lowest Table 2 WER, but the abstract contrasts 6.17% at feature length 60 with the cited DCT 6.45% at length 30; at length 60 DCT is 6.58%. The table therefore supports a better result under its tested settings, while the abstract comparison is not dimension matched.

questions.q: What evaluation conditions are needed to reproduce or interpret the reconstruction and recognition results?
questions.answer: Reconstruction reports random image counts and fixed optimization settings, while speaker/session grouping, seeds, validation/model selection, normalization, and chance-level comparison are omitted. WER conditions also leave test membership, vocabulary/scoring, recognition training, and LM decoding parameters unspecified; repository scripts reveal a directory-order split and validation reuse for reconstruction.

questions.q: Which robustness claims were directly evaluated, and which remain assertions?
questions.answer: The paper reports noisy-input reconstruction and Challenge WER results, but does not report controlled head-motion, imaging-system transfer, or condition-specific robustness tests. Sequence autoencoding and recurrent dynamic modeling are described as future work.

questions.q: Writer: are the target's new Table 2 WERs consistent with whole error counts over the 1023-word SSC test?
questions.answer: Answered by the writer from Ji et al. Table 2 (1023 words; 6.45% = 6+8+52 errors) and the target's Table 2 values: only the two values equal to Ji et al.'s (6.45, 7.72) are k/1023 at two decimals; the eight new values are not (inference). questions.q: Writer: did the target's cited [13] (Jaumard-Hakoun 2016) already use a speckle-noise denoising autoencoder on tongue ultrasound?
questions.answer: Yes: Sec. 3.1 of Jaumard-Hakoun et al. trains the first RBM on speckle-corrupted tongue images (training only); the network is a stacked-RBM fully connected autoencoder. Grep of the specific passage, no reader run.

questions.q: Triage: is 18.7% in Kimura et al. 2020 a WER?
questions.answer: No: Table 1 lists 18.7 as CER without SpecAugment; the best WER is 20.5% (Table 2).

questions.q: Triage: is there an earlier convolutional feature extractor on tongue ultrasound in the wiki?
questions.answer: Yes: Tatulli and Hueber, ICASSP 2017 (supervised CNN on raw ultrasound and video, HMM-GMM). Xu et al. 2017 JASA-EL is not in the wiki. The target does not cite Tatulli.
